parts.move: list the physical factors the drag force on a moving body depends on
parts.prompt: For an object in a regime where drag is modelled by F = ½ρC_DAv², identify how the speed, the fluid and the object's geometry affect the drag force.
scheme: Drag is proportional to the square of the speed v in this model
Drag is proportional to the fluid density ρ
The presented area A and the shape-dependent drag coefficient C_D determine the geometry contribution
parts.answer: In this model, drag is proportional to v² and to the fluid density ρ. The object's geometry enters through its presented cross-sectional area A and its shape-dependent drag coefficient C_D.

parts.move: explain deceleration from speed-dependent drag with no driving force
parts.prompt: A cyclist stops pedalling on level ground and slows down. Explain, in terms of forces, why the deceleration is greatest at first and what happens to the speed.
scheme: With no drive, air resistance is the resultant and it increases with speed
At high speed the backward resultant is large so deceleration is large
As speed falls drag falls, so deceleration decreases toward zero and the bike approaches a steady crawl
parts.answer: Once pedalling stops, drag is the only horizontal force and it grows with speed. The fast bike decelerates hard at first; as it slows, drag and hence deceleration shrink, so the speed levels off instead of dropping to zero abruptly.

parts.move: equate drag to weight for a known mass at terminal velocity
parts.prompt: A 70 kg skydiver falls at terminal velocity. Calculate the drag force on the skydiver. (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
scheme: At terminal velocity the resultant is zero
parts.answer: At terminal velocity drag balances weight: 70 × 9.81 = 687 N, about 690 N upward.

parts.move: counter a mass-only fallacy by naming the drag factors that set terminal speed
parts.prompt: A student claims a 5 kg ball always reaches the ground before a 1 kg ball dropped from the same height in air. Explain why mass alone does not decide this.
scheme: Terminal velocity depends on weight AND drag (area, shape, speed)
A light streamlined object can outfall a heavy flat one; without air both land together
parts.answer: In air, terminal velocity balances weight against drag, which depends on size, shape and speed — not mass alone. A streamlined light object can fall faster than a flat heavy one, and in a vacuum both land together.

parts.move: solve a quadratic drag law for terminal speed
parts.prompt: A 0.50 kg ball experiences drag F = 0.20v² (v in m s⁻¹, F in N). Calculate its terminal velocity. (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
parts.answer: Setting mg = kv² gives v = √(0.50×9.81/0.20) = √24.5 = 4.9 m s⁻¹.

parts.move: combine terminal-velocity force balance with power as rate of energy dissipation
parts.prompt: A raindrop of mass 4.0×10⁻⁶ kg falls at a terminal velocity of 9.0 m s⁻¹. Calculate the rate at which it dissipates energy. (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
parts.answer: The drag equals the weight, 4.0×10⁻⁶ × 9.81 = 3.92×10⁻⁵ N. Dissipated power is Fv = 3.92×10⁻⁵ × 9.0 = 3.5×10⁻⁴ W.
